title: Reiger Fly & Tackle’s Crossroads

scenario.title: Reiger Fly & Tackle’s Crossroads
scenario.setting: Nestled between a salt-crusted clam shack and a driftwood art gallery in coastal La Push, Washington, Reiger Fly & Tackle has operated as a three-generation family shop since 1947. Its weathered clapboard siding is streaked with sea spray and faint rust from decades of displayed casting reels, and the front window balances hand-tied steelhead flies beside dented saltwater tackle passed down from the shop’s original owner. The current owner, Marnie Reiger, received an unexpected 40% rent hike last week, forcing her to choose between leaning into the sustainable fly-tying supplies that draw younger eco-conscious anglers or doubling down on the classic saltwater gear that has kept loyal regulars coming for decades.

characters.name: Marnie Reiger
characters.tendencies: A third-generation shop owner torn between honoring her family’s 75-year legacy and updating the shop’s inventory to survive a sudden, steep rent hike

characters.name: Ernie Reiger
characters.tendencies: A diehard traditionalist who refuses to stock 'fad' fly-tying supplies and insists the shop only sell classic saltwater fishing gear

characters.name: Lila Marquez
characters.tendencies: A local environmental educator and fly fisher who pushes Marnie to stock sustainable fly-tying materials to attract younger, eco-conscious customers and boost the shop’s revenue

characters.name: Jake Torres
characters.tendencies: A middle-aged commercial fisherman and weekly regular who buys both classic saltwater reels and occasional fly-tying supplies for his teen son, uncertain how the shop’s changes will affect his favorite local spot

turns.name: Marnie Reiger
turns.text:
This shop’s been perched on this La Push boardwalk for 75 years, longer than the neighboring salt-crusted clam shack even started serving their famous buttery chowder. I can’t just swap out my great-grandpa’s hand-tied salmon flies and vintage cedar tackle chests for mass-produced, cheap imported gear just to cover this sudden steep rent hike.
[She brushes salt spray off a shelf of hand-carved driftwood lures she’d been testing as a new inventory item before hunching slightly, crumpling the taped-to-the-door rent notice a little more in her calloused fingers.]

turns.name: Ernie Reiger
turns.text:
I don’t stock any of that trendy fad stuff—this shop’s for serious saltwater anglers, not weekend hobbyists chasing viral fishing hacks. A properly tied bucktail jig or spun deer hair dry fly is all you need to hook a chinook or red rockfish, no flimsy plastic nonsense required.
[Slams a dented metal tin of hand-tied classic salmon flies onto the scuffed Formica counter, glowering at the customer who’d laid out a pack of neon micro-synthetic flies on the register.]

turns.name: Lila Marquez
turns.text:
I’ve had three twenty-something and teen anglers ask about sustainable fly-tying materials already this shift. Swapping our stock of cheap synthetic furs for foraged local feathers and naturally shed deer mane would draw in that eco-conscious crowd and boost our bottom line without alienating our regulars.
[I lean across the scuffed, salt-stained wooden counter and tap a glass jar brimming with iridescent, locally harvested abalone shell scraps, which make brilliant, zero-waste bead eyes for hand-tied flies.]

turns.name: Jake Torres
turns.text:
Hey, how’s it goin’? I heard you guys revamped your inventory recently, and I was worried I’d lose access to the Shimano big-game reels I’ve used for my commercial cod runs for years. Also, my teen boy’s been begging for premium wool bug bodies for his fly-tying projects, so I wanted to pick those up too.
[He sets a salt-crusted commercial fishing glove on the scuffed wooden counter, shoving a crumpled, fish-stained note scrawled with his requested items out toward the clerk.]

turns.name: Marnie Reiger
turns.text:
Jake, thank goodness you stopped by—we’re not getting rid of your go-to Shimano big-game reels, not on your or Dad’s watch. We’re just adding a small curated section of sustainable fly-tying supplies to keep up with steady customer demand and cover the sudden rent hike that landed in our mailbox last week.
[Reaches under the scuffed pine counter and pulls out a dented cardboard box stenciled "eco supplies" in fading white paint, its edges crusted with coastal salt from the boardwalk’s sea spray]

turns.name: Ernie Reiger
turns.text:
Sustainable fly materials? That’s a marketing gimmick, not serious tackle. I’ve relied on deer hair and bucktail for 40 years, and this shop won’t stock anything that undercuts the classic gear that’s kept saltwater anglers landing trophy fish for generations. You won’t lose your go-to Shimano big-game reels here—we’re not ditching the reliable stuff for flash-in-the-pan trends.
[He nods toward the wall lined with polished vintage big-game reels, then taps a jar of hand-tied natural bucktail flies bolted to the countertop.]

turns.name: Lila Marquez
turns.text:
"Three of those younger, eco-conscious anglers already asked about sustainable fly-tying supplies this shift, folks who care about protecting the coastal waters we love to fish. Shifting just a portion of our stock to ethically sourced, eco-friendly materials would bring in this loyal, growing customer base without alienating our regular serious saltwater crew."
[I gesture to the clear tackle tray I set on the shop’s counter, filled with hand-tied flies made from recycled sinew and naturally shed local deer hair.]

turns.name: Jake Torres
turns.text:
Hey, how’s it goin’? I heard you guys revamped your inventory recently, and I was worried I’d lose access to the Shimano big-game reels I’ve used for salmon charters out of Neah Bay for the last decade. Figured I’d swing by to confirm you still carry the heavy-duty models I rely on, though my teen son’s been pestering me to pick up some sustainable fly-tying supplies for his own small freshwater projects lately.
[reaches into the frayed canvas tackle bag slung over one shoulder to pull out a crumpled list scrawled on a fish cleaning slip, one side scribbled with reel model numbers and the other with fly-tying material notes]

dm_opening: DM opening: the Marnie Reiger takes a position; the cast gathers around a question the scene has been carrying for a year.
dm_closing: DM closing: the Marnie Reiger still holds the line; the next session's hook — a new member, an old scar — is already at the door.
